newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets seen awakening.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets seen awakening.

text.p: Australian markets should awaken from their Christmas/New Year slumber early this week as 1997 kicks off with a rush of local releases, before attention switches to the U.S. later in the week.
"After a data famine since mid-December, it's a veritable feast this week on the domestic economic front," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.

Monday sees the release of the November current account deficit, which is expected to come in at around A$1.75 billion, close to October's level. Economists said that after stabilising in 1996, the current account may again widen through 1997 if the economy picks up some steam as is widely expected.

The November deficit is seen being stable despite the already reported 1.2 percent rise in imports. After a three month period in surplus in the middle of the year, the trade balance has been in deficit for the last two months. Exports need to rise by 1.6 percent to return the balance to surplus.

Retail trade and building approvals for November follow on Tuesday. Of the economists Reuters surveyed, none were expecting a fall in retail trade, as further correction to September's 3.7 percent fall is expected after the disappointing 1.4 percent rise in October.
Consumer demand is seen remaining soft in underlying terms, although economists said it would be interesting to see if the November and December rate cuts had boosted pre-Christmas spending.

After recent volatility, a fall in building approvals is expected. However the 2.0 percent fall follows a 12.8 percent rise, and the housing sector is expected to show signs of upswing into 1997, moreso as the rate cuts begin to impact.

A forward indicator of the labour market, jobs vacancies and overtime, will be released on Thursday. Not a widely forecast series, it is still closely watched as a complement to other vacancies measures, and the movements in the hours of overtime worked are seen as an indicator of possible changes in production levels, economists said.
Reserve Bank credit aggregates are also due mid-week, before attention turns to the U.S. for the release of December PPI on Thursday and non-farm payrolls on Friday.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri close US$0.7915/20, NY $0.7909/14)

Australian dollar traders will be hoping some depth has returned to the market this week after a thin Christmas New Year period, with Tokyo reopening after holdiays, corporate Australia returning and dealing room staff numbers back to more normal levels.

The two days trading after New Year's Day were deathly quiet in the local session with Tokyo closed, but the data releases early in the week and the lead up to U.S. payrolls on Friday should see activity pick up.
For the Australian dollar, movements in U.S. dollar/yen will be important, as will growing concerns over the prospect of U.S. interest rates rising.

While negative asset market reaction may weaken the U.S. dollar and flow through to the local unit, the Australian dollar will also suffer from the prospect of a narrowing interest differential, traders said.
But first, the dollar has to clear local data hurdles. Despite the strength of support just under US$0.7900 on Friday morning, analysts said the unit still remained vulnerable.
"A poor current account (deficit) on Monday could see it fall temporarily below US$0.7900," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said, adding that the dollar was well suported longer term.

The key support level is US$0.7810 -- the low point of the unit in the last four and a half months -- but before then there is a wide band of support, with important levels at US$0.7890, US$0.7965, and then around US$0.7850.
On the topside, US$0.7925 is the first hurdle ahead of US$0.7950. Above there, there are interim resistance pints on the way to solid wall at US$0.8000, analysts said.
AUSTRALIAN SHARES (Friday All Ords 2,399.5, down 11.7)
The Australian share market is likely to start the week on a positive note after Wall Street stocks stormed higher on Friday, the Dow posting a 101 point or 1.6 percent gain.

Australian shares made steady gains in thin trade last week despite a volatile Dow and dealers said shares were set to continue their upward trend on better volume with most players back to work after a break for Christmas and the new year.
"There is not a lot of local news at the moment and the U.S. will set the tone," said a senior dealer at a Sydney brokerage.

Corporate events of interest include court proceedings for the St George Bank /Advance Bank merger with plenty of people interested to see the position of St George substantial shareholder, National Australia Bank, and the Australian Securities Commission.
The major meeting of interest is recently-listed insurance and financial services group, National Mutual Holdings, whose shareholders meet on Saturday.

Dealers said investors would keep a close eye on a number of economic releases this week with attention focused on November current account data due on Monday and retail trade and building approvals for November on Tuesday.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri 10-yr cash 7.69 pct, 3-yr cash 6.85)
Developments in the U.S. are again likely to be the overriding factor in driving the Australian bond market this week even though the major data flow resumes after year-end.

U.S. Treasuries rose, then gave back most gains in moderate volume on Friday amid fresh speculation the Fed may soon raise official interest rates. Speculation about the Fed's next move should keep the local bond market on its toes this week.

"At the longer end of the yield curve, we are at the whim of the U.S. markets. As long as inflation fears exist in the U.S., bond markets will see rising yields," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank.
Local long-dated yields spiked some 30 basis points in the first two trading days of the year to their highest level since mid-October in sympathy with the U.S. market.

This followed rises in both U.S. housing starts and consumer confidence, and the influential NAPM index jumping close to 55.0, a level that historically has preceded a tightening by the Federal Reserve.

This week's domestic data will give the status on the current account deficit, retail trade prior to Christmas and the state of the building sector, but will not reflect the impact of last month's policy easing by the Reserve Bank, and may not be sufficient to draw the market from its U.S. gaze.

However, the resumption of trading in Japan after a near week long holiday could see a pick-up in local turnover, partically if investors there see the recent weakness in the market as a buying opportunity.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
